Europe lifts sanctions against two Russians

The EU has agreed to remove Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list, while extending restrictions on nearly 3,000 individuals and companies linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine for another three years. The decision came after difficult negotiations, as EU sanctions require unanimous approval from all 27 member states. Caroline Baum reports.

corpus.title: ‘Lifting Restrictions Must Not Become a Precedent,’ Kyiv Says After Russian Billionaires Delisted
corpus.signal_text:
Ukraine has criticized the EU’s decision to remove Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list, with an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky warning that the move could set a precedent for weakening the bloc’s pressure on Moscow.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Zelensky’s adviser on sanctions policy, told Kyiv Post that Ukraine found the EU decision “very strange,” arguing that there was no change in circumstances.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Russia continues the war, and their ties with the Kremlin,which were among the grounds for the sanctions, have not disappeared,” he added.
Ukraine warns against weakening sanctions unity
Vlasiuk said Russia could seek to exploit divisions within the EU over sanctions and warned that removing restrictions from individual Russian businessmen should not become a broader precedent.
“Russia is attempting to fracture EU unity, and it is crucial not to let this crack widen and lead to a weakening of the common sanctions policy,” he said.
“Lifting restrictions on individual Russian businessmen must not become a new precedent,” Vlasiuk added.
He said Kyiv would respond by proposing additional sanctions, particularly against Russian oligarchs linked to the country’s military-industrial complex who have not yet been targeted.
“Right now, it is vital to focus on increasing sanctions pressure on Russia.”
Despite its criticism of the delistings, Kyiv welcomed the EU’s decision to extend the broader sanctions regime for three years.

“At the same time, we appreciate the EU’s decision to extend – for another 36 months – sanctions against individuals and entities responsible for undermining Ukraine’s territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence,” Vlasiuk said.
“This is an important decision that provides the sanctions regime with necessary long-term stability.”
The measures currently cover more than 3,000 individuals and entities and include asset freezes, travel restrictions, and a ban on making funds or economic resources available to those listed.
As part of the decision, however, the EU removed Usmanov and Fridman from the sanctions list, along with another individual and a company. The names of Usmanov and Fridman are explicitly listed in the EU’s implementing regulation.

Azerbaijan pardons French businessman Martin Ryan after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a decree pardoning French businessman Martin Ryan and 19 other people.
In March, a court in Baku sentenced Ryan to 10 years in prison on charges of collecting information about the army during the conflict in Nagorno-Karabakh.
According to media reports, Ryan’s release was part of a deal between Baku and Paris, under which France pushed for EU sanctions on Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be lifted.
The European Union removed Usmanov, as well as a second Russian businessman, Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list on September 22.

corpus.title: EU Removes Billionaires Usmanov and Fridman From Sanctions List
corpus.signal_text:
EU diplomats agreed Tuesday to drop billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the bloc's Russian sanctions list and to roll over the remaining 3,000 individuals and entities for another three years.
Earlier this month, France shocked other EU members when it pushed for Russian-Uzbek metals tycoon Usmanov to be removed from EU sanctions, citing national security concerns. Luxembourg then demanded the same treatment for Fridman, who has launched a $16 billion claim against the country.
As a compromise, EU envoys agreed to remove the two billionaires in exchange for a three-year renewal of measures against the other sanctioned individuals and entities instead of the usual six months.
Latvia was the last holdout in an unusually fraught process. The deadline to renew the sanctions was at midnight on Sept. 22 after an extension from the original expiry on September 15.
Sanctions require unanimity among EU countries to be approved. Latvia ultimately abstained, diplomats said, which allowed the deal to pass. The decision was formally approved via a process known as a written procedure later on Tuesday.
"The decision to delist Usmanov and Fridman is shameful and unjustifiable. Moscow is celebrating," Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X, urging EU countries to impose their own national restrictions on the two men.
Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said Riga would look to impose its own sanctions. He added that France had agreed to start talks with Latvia about joining a French nuclear deterrence initiative.
The episode has roiled European leaders who had hoped to present a more united front against Russia since a recent change of government in Hungary. Former Hungarian leader Viktor Orban was a frequent obstacle to sanctions and support for Ukraine.
It took high-level meetings in Europe and on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week to iron out the agreement, diplomats said.
The EU imposed sanctions on both men in 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which include transaction and travel bans in the EU and a freeze on assets held in the bloc.
Latvia had previously taken legal action to maintain EU sanctions on Fridman and his Russian-Latvian business partner Petr Aven. For Riga, Fridman's connection to Aven is a sore point, diplomats said.
Aven was stripped of the country's highest civilian honor in 2022 for not condemning Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

corpus.title: Latvian PM says Latvia was only EU country to oppose lifting of sanctions on Russian oligarchs
corpus.signal_text:
Latvian PM says Latvia was only EU country to oppose lifting of sanctions on Russian oligarchs
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs has said Latvia was the only EU country to oppose the lifting of sanctions on Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
Source: Baltic states news website Delfi, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Kulbergs' comments concerned the EU's decision to remove Russian oligarchs Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov from its sanctions list.
He believes the issue of extending the sanctions should have been resolved in a way that would not leave Latvia isolated. He added that the Baltic states should also have agreed on a common position.
The Latvian prime minister said that "the goal should have been to achieve an outcome in which Latvia would not become the last country in Europe left alone".
He noted that all EU member states had reached an agreement, leaving Latvia as the only country opposed to the lifting of sanctions on Usmanov and Fridman.
Kulbergs added that, to his surprise, Lithuania and Estonia had already agreed to remove the two men from the sanctions list. He stressed that the Baltic states should maintain a common position and that the issue needed to be resolved.
"The choice was tough: either a really bad situation or simply a bad one," the prime minister said.
He was also surprised that Latvia's interests had effectively never been discussed.
The prime minister said Latvia had remained firm in its position and had not given its consent, but had been forced to abstain rather than vote against the decision as a whole.
Background:
- The EU extended restrictive measures against individuals responsible for undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence for another 36 months, but removed Usmanov and Fridman from the sanctions list.
- It was reported that France planned to "exchange" Usmanov's delisting for the release of several French citizens who are currently in prison in Azerbaijan.
- Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the move "shameful".
